# Docker for Reproducibility {#sec-docker}

Two analysts ran the same bootstrap script, from the same commit
and with the same seed, and reported different confidence
intervals for the same trial. Neither had made an error. One
machine ran R 3.5 and the other R 3.6, and R 3.6.0 changed the
algorithm `sample()` uses to draw integers, so the same seed
produced different resamples. The difference sat in the second
decimal place, small enough to pass for rounding and large enough
to change a table a reviewer had already seen. `renv` could not
have caught it, because no package changed; the R build beneath
the packages did. A container fixes R, the system libraries, and
the operating system along with the packages, so that the same
code gives the same number on every machine that runs the image.

::: {.bookepigraph}
```{=latex}
\begin{flushright}\small
```
*But it works on my machine.*

[A folk theorem of software]{.smallcaps} (n.d.)
```{=latex}
\end{flushright}
```
:::

```{r}

#| include: false
source('_pipeline.R')
```

## Images, containers, and layers {#sec-docker-model}

### What `renv` leaves out

`renv` pins the R packages, and R packages are not the whole
environment. Beneath them sit the R build itself, the system
libraries packages compile against, and the operating system
(OS), none of which the lockfile installs. Most of the time this
does not matter, which is exactly why it is easy to overlook. The
chunk below reproduces the opening on the HF-HOME trial: it
bootstraps the 30-day risk difference, in percentage points, with
the same seed under the integer sampler R used before version 3.6.0
and the one it has used since.

```{r}
#| label: docker-same-code
hf_dir <- file.path('..', 'data', 'raw_data', 'hfhome')
rand <- read.csv(file.path(hf_dir, 'randomization.csv'),
                 colClasses = c(patient_id = 'character'))
outc <- read.csv(file.path(hf_dir, 'outcomes.csv'),
                 colClasses = c(patient_id = 'character'))
hf <- merge(rand[c('patient_id', 'arm')],
            outc[c('patient_id', 'event_30d')], by = 'patient_id')
stopifnot(nrow(hf) == nrow(rand))
hf <- hf[!is.na(hf$event_30d), ]
usual <- hf$event_30d[hf$arm == 'Usual care']
home <- hf$event_30d[hf$arm == 'Home health']

boot_rd <- function(sample_kind, reps = 2000, seed = 2019) {
  old <- RNGkind()
  on.exit(RNGkind(old[1], old[2], old[3]))
  suppressWarnings(RNGkind(sample.kind = sample_kind))
  set.seed(seed)
  rd <- replicate(reps, {
    mean(sample(usual, replace = TRUE)) -
      mean(sample(home, replace = TRUE))
  })
  100 * quantile(rd, c(0.025, 0.975))
}

intervals <- rbind(r_before_3_6 = boot_rd('Rounding'),
                   r_3_6_and_later = boot_rd('Rejection'))
round(intervals, 2)
```

Same data, same seed, same resampling code, and only the sampler
differs, as it does between R 3.5 and any R since 3.6.0: the lower
bound moves from
`r sprintf('%.2f', intervals[1, 1])` to
`r sprintf('%.2f', intervals[2, 1])`. Both intervals include zero,
as the trial's result is inconclusive, but a reader comparing your
table with a rerun sees two different numbers and no explanation.
The `sample.kind` argument lets one R imitate the other here; a
change in a system linear-algebra library offers no such switch,
and it can move the last digits of a regression coefficient
between two machines with identical lockfiles. Docker closes the
gap by specifying the whole stack rather than its top layer.

The cost is a second technology to learn and a build step to wait
for. It is worth paying for work that must reproduce years later,
and for work that depends on system libraries at all. It is not
worth paying for a self-contained analysis that will be finished
this quarter. The case for containers in research computing was
made by Boettiger [-@boettiger2015introduction], and it is the
argument this chapter assumes.

### The mental model

| Term | What it is | What follows |
|---|---|---|
| Image | An immutable, read-only template: OS, system libraries, R, packages, code | The artifact you build, share, and archive |
| Container | A running instance of an image, with a writable layer on top | Changes made inside it vanish when it is removed |
| Layer | The result of one `RUN`, `COPY`, or `ADD` instruction | Cached and reused, which is why order matters |
| Registry | A server that stores images (Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry) | Hosting, not archiving (@sec-docker-sharing) |
| Tag | A movable name for an image, such as `4.4.0` | Can be rebuilt to point at different bytes |
| Digest | The content hash of an image, `sha256:...` | The only identifier that cannot move |

: Docker's vocabulary. {#tbl-docker-terms}

On an Apple Silicon Mac, add `--platform linux/amd64` to every
`docker pull`, `docker run`, and `docker build`. Many R images
and binary package repositories target x86_64 only, and an image
built for arm64 will not run on a typical Linux server; see
@tbl-docker-failures. Every command in this chapter carries the
flag, which costs nothing on an Intel machine.

The everyday commands (display-only):

```bash
docker pull --platform linux/amd64 rocker/r-ver:4.4.0
docker run -it --rm --platform linux/amd64 rocker/r-ver:4.4.0 R
docker run -it --rm --platform linux/amd64 -v "$(pwd)":/work \
  rocker/r-ver:4.4.0 R               # with the project mounted
docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t my-analysis:v1.0 .
docker images                        # list local images
docker rmi my-analysis:v1.0          # remove an image
```

The `--rm` flag removes the container when it exits; without it,
stopped containers accumulate.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Confirm that the image gives you the R and the OS you expect,
whatever your laptop runs:

```bash
docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 rocker/r-ver:4.4.0 R --version
docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 rocker/r-ver:4.4.0 \
  grep PRETTY /etc/os-release
```

The first should begin `R version 4.4.0`, and the second should
name Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (long-term support), the base of the
`rocker/r-ver` 4.4 images. If you see your laptop's R version,
you ran R outside the container.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** You build an image `readmissions:v1.0`, run a
container from it, install a new R package inside the running
container, then exit. Is the package available the next time you
run a container from the same image?

**Answer.** No. The image is immutable; changes inside a container
live only in its writable layer, which is discarded when the
container is removed (at exit, with `--rm`). To add the package
permanently, install it in the project, snapshot `renv.lock`, and
rebuild the image. This is the discipline that makes Docker a
reproducibility tool: changes happen in the Dockerfile and the
lockfile, in version control, never in running containers. 'Works
on my machine' becomes 'works on this image, which everyone has'.
:::

## Choosing and pinning a base image {#sec-docker-rocker}

### The `rocker` images

The `rocker` project [@boettiger2017rocker] maintains the standard
R images at [rocker-project.org](https://rocker-project.org/).
Each builds on the one before it and is tagged with its R version:

| Image | Adds | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| `rocker/r-ver` | R on Ubuntu LTS (about 0.8 GB) | `renv`-based projects that install their own packages; continuous integration |
| `rocker/rstudio` | RStudio Server | Interactive work in a browser |
| `rocker/tidyverse` | The tidyverse and common dependencies (about 3 GB) | Teaching, and quick starts where most projects use the tidyverse |
| `rocker/verse` | TeX and publishing tools | Rendering PDF documents |
| `rocker/geospatial` | GDAL, GEOS, and PROJ, the spatial system libraries | Spatial analysis |
| `bioconductor/bioconductor_docker` | Bioconductor's toolchain | Genomics |

: Base images for R. Sizes are approximate and uncompressed, as
observed for recent tags. {#tbl-docker-rocker}

Pick the smallest base that has your prerequisites. A larger base
is convenient during development and costs build time, disk, and
a larger surface of things that can change underneath you. For a
compendium whose packages are pinned by `renv`, `rocker/r-ver` is
the right base: the lockfile, not the image, decides the
packages.

### Tags, digests, and what each pins

`FROM rocker/r-ver:4.4.0` pins the R version; `FROM
rocker/r-ver:latest` drifts. Neither pins the bytes. Only a digest
does:

```dockerfile
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.4.0@sha256:73adabf378930f8744f56bac1fe5e99870532eb4ced1a15075991bac909d21f3
```

The same reasoning applies to system packages installed with
`apt-get`: either pin their versions, or accept that a rebuild
months later installs newer ones. A digest-pinned base fixes the
packages that come with the base; it cannot fix what a later
`apt-get update` fetches.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Find the digest of a tag you have pulled:

```bash
docker inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' rocker/r-ver:4.4.0
```

It prints `rocker/r-ver@sha256:` followed by 64 hexadecimal
characters. Paste the hash after the tag in your `FROM` line, as
above, and rebuild; the build log's `FROM` step now names the
digest.
:::

### Exercises

1. Choose a base image from @tbl-docker-rocker for each project.
   (a) A trial analysis whose `renv.lock` pins every package,
   rendered to HTML. (b) The same analysis, rendered to PDF.
   (c) A course in which forty students need RStudio in a browser
   on the first day. (d) A spatial analysis of ZIP-code-level
   readmission rates with `sf`.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
(a) `rocker/r-ver` at the R version in the lockfile: the lockfile
supplies the packages, so a larger base only adds things to drift.
(b) Still `rocker/r-ver`, plus `quarto install tinytex` in the
Dockerfile (@sec-docker-canonical); `rocker/verse` also works and
is larger. (c) `rocker/tidyverse`, which includes RStudio Server
and the packages a course needs, so that the first day is not
spent installing. (d) `rocker/r-ver` with the spatial system
libraries added to the `apt-get` line, as in the worked example
(@sec-docker-worked), or `rocker/geospatial` if you prefer to
inherit them.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Your Dockerfile begins `FROM rocker/verse:4.4.1`.
That is an exact version, not `latest`. Does rebuilding it in two
years give you the same image?

**Answer.** Probably not. A tag is a movable label, not a fixed
identity. `4.4.1` pins the R version, and the maintainers can and
do rebuild that tag against a newer Ubuntu base, refreshed apt
packages, and patched system libraries; your `FROM` line resolves
to whatever the tag points at today. The digest cannot change: if
it resolves at all, it resolves to exactly the bytes you built
against.

The trade-off is real. A pinned digest never picks up a security
patch, so it ages into a liability, and the hash is unreadable in
a diff. The usual compromise is a version tag during development
and a digest recorded at the moment of submission, alongside the
`sap-v1.0` tag of @sec-analysis-plan, so the archived artifact is
reconstructible even though day-to-day work is not frozen.
Archiving the built image (@sec-docker-sharing) sidesteps the
question entirely.
:::

## A research-compendium Dockerfile {#sec-docker-canonical}

This is the book's one canonical Dockerfile; @sec-rrtools and
@sec-renv use it unchanged. It assumes the compendium layout of
@sec-rrtools, a `renv.lock` that includes `rmarkdown` and `knitr`
(Quarto needs both to run R chunks), and the `.Rprofile` and
`renv/activate.R` that `renv::init()` writes.

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.4.0

ARG QUARTO_VERSION=1.6.40

RUN apt-get update \
  && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    ca-certificates curl \
    libcurl4-openssl-dev libssl-dev libxml2-dev libuv1-dev \
  && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# rocker/r-ver ships R but not the Quarto CLI
RUN arch="$(dpkg --print-architecture)" \
  && curl -fsSL -o /tmp/quarto.deb \
    "https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/releases/download/v${QUARTO_VERSION}/quarto-${QUARTO_VERSION}-linux-${arch}.deb" \
  && dpkg -i /tmp/quarto.deb \
  && rm /tmp/quarto.deb

# outside /work, so a bind mount of the project cannot hide it
ENV RENV_PATHS_LIBRARY=/opt/renv/library

WORKDIR /work
COPY renv.lock .Rprofile ./
COPY renv/activate.R renv/activate.R
RUN R -q -e "renv::restore(prompt = FALSE)"

COPY . .

CMD ["quarto", "render", "analysis/paper/paper.qmd"]
```

### Three details that are easy to get wrong

- **Quarto is not in the base image.** `rocker/r-ver` does not
  include the Quarto command line interface (CLI), so the image
  installs a pinned release; without it, `quarto render` fails.
- **The render command is `quarto render`.** `rmarkdown::render()`
  is the R Markdown renderer and does not process a `.qmd`
  project.
- **The base tag must match the R version in `renv.lock`.**
  Otherwise `renv` restores the right packages onto the wrong R.

For the strongest pin, replace the tag with the digest, as in
@sec-docker-rocker. The image above renders HTML; for PDF output,
add `RUN quarto install tinytex --no-prompt` after the Quarto
layer.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**A base image that does not match the lockfile builds without
error.** `renv::restore()` installs the recorded package versions
onto whatever R the image has, notes the mismatch in one line of a
build log nobody reads (`Using R 4.4.0 (lockfile was generated
with R 4.6.1)`), and the image renders. The packages are pinned and R is
not, which is the gap the opening described. Read the R version
from the lockfile before you write the `FROM` line:
`renv::lockfile_read('renv.lock')$R$Version`.
:::

### `.dockerignore`

Next to the Dockerfile, commit a `.dockerignore`. It keeps the
local package library, credentials, and other machine-specific
files out of the build context, and therefore out of an image you
may later push to a public registry:

```
.git/
.Rproj.user/
.Rhistory
.RData
.Renviron
.env
secrets/
renv/library/
renv/staging/
renv/local/
_freeze/
```

Without it, `COPY . .` copies your `.Renviron`, with whatever API
tokens it holds, into a layer of the image, and deleting the file
in a later layer does not remove it from the earlier one.

### Layer order

The order of the Dockerfile is lockfile, then restore, then project
source, and @fig-docker-layers shows why. Docker caches each layer
and reuses it on the next build unless that layer or something
above it has changed. Copying the lockfile and restoring packages
*before* copying the frequently edited manuscript means that an
ordinary day of writing invalidates only the fast final `COPY`,
leaving the slow package-restore layer untouched.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-docker-layers
%%| fig-alt: "Vertical stack of Dockerfile layers in build order,
%%|   annotated by how often each changes. A cached rocker/r-ver
%%|   base, then system dependencies that rarely change, then
%%|   copying renv.lock and restoring packages, which changes when
%%|   packages change, then copying the source tree, which changes
%%|   on every edit, then the render command. The last two layers
%%|   are highlighted in contrasting colors to mark the cache
%%|   boundary."
%%| fig-cap: "Docker layer caching. Slow, slow-changing layers go early;
%%|   the fast, frequently-edited source goes last. Editing the
%%|   manuscript invalidates only the final COPY, so the expensive
%%|   package restore is reused from cache."
flowchart TD
  A["FROM rocker/r-ver<br/><i>cached base image</i>"] --> B["RUN apt-get system deps<br/><i>rarely changes</i>"]
  B --> C["COPY renv.lock + restore<br/><i>changes when packages change</i>"]
  C --> D["COPY . /work<br/><i>changes every edit</i>"]
  D --> E["CMD quarto render"]
  style C fill:#e8f4f4,stroke:#2c7a7b
  style D fill:#fbe9e7,stroke:#9d2235
```

### Building and running

From the compendium root (display-only):

```bash
docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t readmissions:v1.0 .
docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 \
  -v "$(pwd)/analysis/paper:/work/analysis/paper" \
  readmissions:v1.0
```

`quarto render` writes its output next to the source, in
`/work/analysis/paper/`, so that is the directory to mount. The
rendered file then appears in your host's `analysis/paper/`; a
mount at any other container path receives nothing.

Data follow the same choice. Copying data into the image makes it
self-contained and larger; mounting them keeps the image small and
means the image alone no longer reproduces the analysis. Embed
small, shareable data; mount large or sensitive data, and never
build an image containing protected health information that might
reach a registry.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Check the cache and the environment, not only that the build
succeeded:

```bash
docker build --progress=plain --platform linux/amd64 \
  -t readmissions:v1.0 . 2>&1 | grep -A1 'renv::restore'
docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 readmissions:v1.0 R --version
docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 readmissions:v1.0 \
  Rscript -e 'renv::status()'
```

After you edit a `.qmd` file and rebuild, the line after the
`renv::restore` step should read `CACHED`; if the step runs again,
the layer order is wrong. `R --version` should match the
lockfile's `R$Version`, and `renv::status()` should report no
issues. A mismatched base tag shows up here as a status message
that the lockfile was generated with a different R.
:::

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
> **Context.** My compendium's `renv.lock` records R
> `<output of renv::lockfile_read('renv.lock')$R$Version>` and the
> packages listed below. The paper renders with
> `quarto render analysis/paper/paper.qmd`. The project tree is:
> `<output of tree -L 2>`.
>
> **Constraints.** Base the image on `rocker/r-ver` at the tag
> equal to that R version, with a `FROM` line pinned by digest (I
> will fill in the digest from `docker inspect`; do not invent
> one). Install a pinned Quarto CLI release. Copy `renv.lock`,
> `.Rprofile`, and `renv/activate.R` and restore before copying
> the project. Write a `.dockerignore` that excludes `.git/`,
> `.Renviron`, `.env`, and `renv/library/`. Add only the system
> libraries my packages need, and say which package needs each.
>
> **Criteria.** The image builds with `--platform linux/amd64`;
> after I edit a `.qmd` file and rebuild, the restore step is
> `CACHED`; inside the container, `R --version` matches the
> lockfile and `renv::status()` reports no issues.

*Failure mode.* Models write a base tag from their training data
(`rocker/r-ver:4.4.0`, or `latest`) that does not match your
lockfile, invent a plausible-looking digest, omit the
`.dockerignore`, or copy the whole project before the restore so
that every edit reinstalls every package. *Check.* Run the
Verification above, and compare the draft line by line with the
canonical Dockerfile. The prompt carries file names and package
names, not data (@sec-ai-governance).
:::

### Exercises

2. A colleague's Dockerfile reads, in order: `FROM
   rocker/r-ver:latest`; `COPY . /work`; `RUN R -q -e
   "renv::restore(prompt = FALSE)"`; `CMD ["Rscript", "-e",
   "rmarkdown::render('analysis/paper/paper.qmd')"]`. There is no
   `.dockerignore`. List every problem and the fix for each.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
- `latest` drifts: use the tag equal to the lockfile's R version,
  pinned by digest at submission.
- `COPY . /work` before the restore invalidates the restore layer
  on every edit: copy `renv.lock`, `.Rprofile`, and
  `renv/activate.R` first, restore, then `COPY . .`.
- Without a `.dockerignore`, the build context includes
  `renv/library/` (slow, and the wrong platform's binaries) and
  any `.Renviron` or `.env`, which then sit in a layer of an image
  that may be pushed publicly.
- `rmarkdown::render()` does not render a Quarto project, and
  `rocker/r-ver` has no Quarto: install a pinned Quarto CLI and
  use `CMD ["quarto", "render", "analysis/paper/paper.qmd"]`.
- With the library inside `/work`, a bind mount of the project
  would hide it: set `RENV_PATHS_LIBRARY` outside `/work`.

The canonical Dockerfile above is the corrected file.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** You add one package to `renv.lock` and rebuild.
Which layers rebuild, and why is that correct?

**Answer.** The two `COPY` layers that bring in `renv.lock` and its
bootstrap files change, so the restore layer and everything after
it rebuild; the base image, the system libraries, and the Quarto
install are reused from cache. That is the intended behavior: a
dependency change should reinstall packages, and an edit to the
manuscript should not.
:::

## Interactive and multi-service containers {#sec-docker-rstudio}

### RStudio Server in a container

For interactive work in a pinned environment, run RStudio Server
from a `rocker` image (display-only):

```bash
docker run -d --rm --platform linux/amd64 \
  -p 127.0.0.1:8787:8787 \
  -e PASSWORD="$RSTUDIO_PASSWORD" \
  -v "$(pwd)":/home/rstudio/project \
  --name analysis-rstudio \
  rocker/tidyverse:4.4.0
```

Set `RSTUDIO_PASSWORD` in your shell first, rather than typing a
password into a command that lands in your shell history. Binding
to `127.0.0.1` keeps the server off your network; a bare `-p
8787:8787` publishes it on every interface, so anyone who can
reach your machine can try the login. Then open
`http://localhost:8787` and log in as `rstudio`. Your project is
mounted under `/home/rstudio/project`; inside the container, run
`renv::restore()` to install its packages. The pattern suits
teaching (every student gets the same environment) and
collaborative analysis.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Confirm where the server is listening:

```bash
docker port analysis-rstudio
```

It should print `8787/tcp -> 127.0.0.1:8787`. An address of
`0.0.0.0` means the server is reachable from your network; stop
the container and restart it with the `127.0.0.1:` prefix.
:::

### Several services: a pointer to Compose

When an analysis needs a second service, such as a PostgreSQL
database, Docker Compose starts several containers from one
`compose.yaml` file. Three rules prevent most of its problems.
Read passwords from a `.env` file beside the Compose file
(`POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?set it in .env}`), list
`.env` in both `.gitignore` and `.dockerignore`, and never write a
password into the committed file. Use the `docker compose`
subcommand: the hyphenated `docker-compose` binary is Compose
version 1, which reached end of life in 2023, and the top-level
`version:` key older examples show is obsolete. Docker's Compose
documentation covers the rest. For most biostatistical analyses a
single container is enough.

## Sharing and archiving an image {#sec-docker-sharing}

Push the image to a registry so that collaborators can pull it
(display-only):

```bash
docker tag readmissions:v1.0 ghcr.io/username/readmissions:v1.0
docker push ghcr.io/username/readmissions:v1.0

# a reader
docker pull --platform linux/amd64 ghcr.io/username/readmissions:v1.0
docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 ghcr.io/username/readmissions:v1.0
```

Docker Hub works the same way with `username/readmissions:v1.0`. A
registry is hosting, not archiving: accounts lapse, free tiers
change, and images are deleted. For the archival copy, save the
built image as a file and deposit it with the compendium, for
example on Zenodo, which issues a DOI (digital object identifier):

```bash
docker save readmissions:v1.0 | gzip > readmissions-v1.0.tar.gz
# upload readmissions-v1.0.tar.gz to Zenodo with the compendium
```

The saved image is the environment itself, not instructions for
rebuilding it, so it survives the base image's tag being rebuilt,
the apt mirrors moving on, and the registry disappearing. Record
the image ID and the base digest in the compendium's README at
submission.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Confirm that the archive restores the image you built:

```bash
docker image inspect --format '{{.Id}}' readmissions:v1.0
docker rmi readmissions:v1.0
docker load -i readmissions-v1.0.tar.gz
docker image inspect --format '{{.Id}}' readmissions:v1.0
```

`docker load` reads the gzipped file directly. The two IDs must be
identical; then run the loaded image and compare the rendered
paper with yours.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A reviewer asks you to reproduce a table two years
after submission. You have the Dockerfile with a version tag, and
the image on a registry under an account that has lapsed. What can
you reproduce, and what would have made it exact?

**Answer.** You can rebuild from the Dockerfile, but the tag may
now point at a different base and `apt-get` will fetch newer system
libraries, so you get a close environment, not the same one. The
exact environment needed either the archived image file, which
restores the identical bytes, or at least a digest-pinned `FROM`
line, which fixes the base. With either, the R build and system
libraries are those that produced the table.
:::

## Diagnosing build failures {#sec-docker-failures}

Most build failures are one of five kinds, and each has a
recognizable symptom:

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `cannot find -lcurl`, `fatal error: openssl/ssl.h`, or a `configure` error naming a library | A system library is missing for a package that compiles from source (`curl`, `xml2`, `openssl`, `httr2`, `sf` are common) | Add the matching `lib*-dev` package to the `apt-get install` line |
| Every edit reinstalls every package | The project is copied before the restore | Copy the lockfile and bootstrap files first (@fig-docker-layers) |
| The image is gigabytes larger than expected | `apt-get` without `--no-install-recommends`, or the apt lists left behind | Use the install-and-clean pattern of the canonical Dockerfile |
| `exec format error` on a server | Built for arm64 on Apple Silicon, run on x86_64 | Build with `--platform linux/amd64`, or build for both |
| `renv::status()` in the container reports a different R | The base tag does not match the lockfile | Set the `FROM` tag to the lockfile's `R$Version` |

: Docker build failures. {#tbl-docker-failures}

To build one image for both architectures and push it
(display-only):

```bash
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
  -t ghcr.io/username/readmissions:v1.0 --push .
```

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
> **Context.** A `docker build` of the Dockerfile below fails.
> Here are the Dockerfile and the last 40 lines of the build log,
> from the first line containing `ERROR` or `error:`.
>
> **Constraints.** Do not change the base image, the layer order,
> or the R version, and do not suggest installing packages
> outside `renv`. Propose the smallest change.
>
> **Criteria.** Name the R package whose installation failed, the
> system library it needs, and the Ubuntu package that provides
> that library, quoting the log line that shows it.

*Failure mode.* A model that cannot read the cause from a
truncated log proposes a different base image or a long list of
`lib*-dev` packages, which makes the build pass and the image
larger without saying why. *Check.* Rebuild with the one added
package; the failing step should now complete, and the log line
the model quoted should be the one that named the missing
library.
:::

### Exercises

3. Map each error to the Ubuntu package that fixes it.
   (a) `configuration failed for package 'xml2'` with `libxml-2.0
   was not found`. (b) `gdal-config: not found` while installing
   `sf`. (c) `ERROR: dependency 'openssl' is not available`,
   preceded by `ssl.h: No such file or directory`.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
(a) `libxml2-dev`. (b) `libgdal-dev`; `sf` also needs
`libproj-dev` and `libgeos-dev`, so add all three, as in the
worked example. (c) `libssl-dev`. The canonical Dockerfile already
installs (a) and (c), so a log showing either means the line was
edited away. In each case the log names the library or the header
file; the fix is the Ubuntu `-dev` package that provides it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** An image built on your Apple Silicon Mac runs there
and fails on the department's Linux server with `exec format
error`. Your colleague suggests reinstalling Docker on the server.
What is the actual cause?

**Answer.** The image was built for arm64, your laptop's
architecture, and the server is x86_64. Docker is working
correctly on both machines. Rebuild with `--platform linux/amd64`,
or build a multi-architecture image with `docker buildx`.
:::

## Worked example: a dockerized compendium {#sec-docker-worked}

Start from the canonical Dockerfile. A compendium that also uses
`sf` needs the geospatial system libraries, so extend the
`apt-get` line and change nothing else:

```dockerfile
RUN apt-get update \
  && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    ca-certificates curl \
    libcurl4-openssl-dev libssl-dev libxml2-dev libuv1-dev \
    libgdal-dev libproj-dev libgeos-dev \
  && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
```

Build, run, and share (display-only):

```bash
docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t readmissions:v1.0 .
docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 \
  -v "$(pwd)/analysis/paper:/work/analysis/paper" \
  readmissions:v1.0
docker tag readmissions:v1.0 ghcr.io/username/readmissions:v1.0
docker push ghcr.io/username/readmissions:v1.0
```

A reader, given the GitHub repository of the compendium, runs:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/username/readmissions.git
cd readmissions
docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t readmissions:v1.0 .
docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 \
  -v "$(pwd)/analysis/paper:/work/analysis/paper" \
  readmissions:v1.0
```

The paper renders. The reader now has the same R version, the
same package versions, and the same system libraries as of the day
they built, which is close to your environment but not identical
to it: the tag may have been rebuilt since (@sec-docker-rocker).
For an identical environment, give the reader the digest-pinned
Dockerfile or the archived image.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
The reader's check is the one the opening needed: the same number.
Compare the key estimate in the reader's rendered paper with the
one in yours, and the environments behind them:

```bash
docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 readmissions:v1.0 \
  Rscript -e 'sessionInfo()'
```

The R version, platform, and BLAS (Basic Linear Algebra
Subprograms) library lines should match the ones recorded at
submission. If the estimates differ and the environments match,
the cause is in the code or the data, not the machine.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **Habit 4: pin the environment.** The lockfile pins the
   packages; the image pins R, the system libraries, and the OS,
   and only a digest or an archived image pins the bytes.
2. **Habit 8: a plausible number is the expensive bug.** A
   different R or BLAS produces a different number without an
   error; check the R version and `renv::status()` inside the
   container, not only that the build succeeded.
3. **Habit 3: tag what you submit.** Record the base digest and the
   image ID with the Git tag, and archive the image beside the
   compendium; a registry is hosting, not archiving.

## Cumulative practice

4. *Cumulative (uses @sec-renv).* Take a project with a committed
   `renv.lock`. Write its Dockerfile from the canonical one, with
   the `FROM` tag read from the lockfile and pinned by digest, and
   a `.dockerignore`. Build it, edit a `.qmd` file, rebuild, and
   record the evidence that the restore layer was cached. Then run
   `renv::status()` and `R --version` inside the container.
5. *On your own work (no key).* Dockerize an analysis of yours
   that you will need to reproduce after submission. Archive the
   image with `docker save`, remove it, load it again, and confirm
   the image ID and a key number in the output match.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
4. The evidence is the build log line after the `renv::restore`
   step reading `CACHED` on the second build, an `R --version`
   matching `renv::lockfile_read('renv.lock')$R$Version`, and
   `renv::status()` reporting no issues. If `status()` reports that
   the lockfile was generated with a different R, the `FROM` tag
   is wrong. If packages are reported as not installed, the
   restore failed partway, usually for a missing system library
   that the build log names (@tbl-docker-failures).
:::

## Cheat sheet

| Task | Command | Guards against |
|---|---|---|
| Run R in a pinned image | `docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 rocker/r-ver:4.4.0 R` | Your laptop's R leaking into results |
| Find a digest | `docker inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' <image>` | A tag that moves |
| Build for the server | `docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t name:v1 .` | `exec format error` |
| Check the cache | `docker build --progress=plain ...` | Reinstalling every package on every edit |
| Check the environment | `docker run ... Rscript -e 'renv::status()'` | Right packages on the wrong R |
| Keep secrets out | `.dockerignore` with `.Renviron`, `.env`, `renv/library/` | Credentials in a pushed image |
| RStudio, local only | `-p 127.0.0.1:8787:8787` | A login page open to the network |
| Share | `docker push ghcr.io/<user>/<image>:<tag>` | Collaborators rebuilding by hand |
| Archive | `docker save`, compressed with `gzip` | A registry or base tag that changes |
| Restore an archive | `docker load -i image.tar.gz` | Unverified archives |

: Docker at a glance. {#tbl-docker-cheat-sheet}

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-09}

1. A Docker image is an immutable read-only template that includes
   an OS, system libraries, and application code. A container is a
   running instance of an image, with its own writable filesystem
   layer. Many containers can be run from one image; removing a
   container does not modify the image. The image is the artifact;
   the container is the process.
2. `renv` captures R packages only. Docker captures the operating
   system, system libraries (BLAS, geospatial libraries,
   compilers), the R build itself, *and* R packages. When an
   analysis depends on a specific OS or system library, Docker
   comes far closer than `renv` alone to reproducing it years
   later, and a digest-pinned or archived image closer still. For
   pure-R analyses `renv` may suffice; for anything with non-R
   dependencies, Docker is the prudent choice.
3. `rocker/tidyverse:4.4.0` provides Ubuntu LTS (the base of the
   `rocker/r-ver` images it builds on; 22.04 for this tag), R
   4.4.0, RStudio Server, and the tidyverse packages
   pre-installed. A container starts immediately without package
   installation, which suits teaching and quick collaborative
   work. It is larger than `rocker/r-ver`, a trade-off justified
   when most projects use the tidyverse anyway.
